# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a strong follow-up. It does most of what the earlier reviews asked for:
- a registered confirmatory test of the meetings mechanism, filed before the 24-month outcomes were available;
- a second hours measure that does not depend on what staff claim on timesheets;
- like-for-like comparison of the timesheet measure at 9 and 24 months;
- control-group waiting times for the counter arm;
- disclosure that the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours.

The arithmetic checks: 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8%, 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%, 96.8/0.866 gives +11.8%, and the mediation shares sum to 100%.

The main problems are a Summary that overstates the decline, contamination of the control arm that the paper reports but doesn't connect to its estimates, and a mediation result described more strongly than its design allows.

## 1. The Summary compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". But 12.5% is the timesheet measure and 8.5% is the log measure. Comparing like with like on timesheets, the gain went from 12.5% to 9.8%, which the body correctly calls the like-for-like comparison. The Summary's framing makes the decline look like 32% instead of about 22%.

Even the like-for-like decline is not established. The confidence intervals overlap heavily: +6.9 to +18.4 at nine months against +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months. The paper should report a test of the change itself. Without one, "declined but not disappeared" should be "may have declined; has not disappeared".

## 2. The meeting audit contaminated the control arm

Two of the seven control offices cut meetings from month 15, and their output per hour rose 4.1%. The paper presents this as evidence about mechanism, but it also affects the main estimate:

- **Rough size of the effect.** If those two offices are roughly average in size, the control arm's output per hour rose by about 1.2% (2/7 × 4.1%) over the last nine months. The difference-in-differences estimate shrinks correspondingly.
- **Consequence for the decline.** That could account for a substantial part of the 2.7-point fall between 9 and 24 months. Some of the apparent decay may come from the control group improving, not from the treatment effect fading.
- **What to report.** A sensitivity analysis is needed: estimates excluding the two offices, or ending at month 15.

There is also a figure to check. The control arm's average meeting time fell only from 7.2 to 7.0 hours, but two offices fell by 2.1 hours each. So the other five must have risen by about 0.5 hours each on average. That is possible, but it should be confirmed or explained.

## 3. The mediation result doesn't "confirm" the mechanism

**It is not an independent test.** The registration came after the hypothesis was generated, using the same seven treated offices whose correlation (r = 0.71) prompted it. Registering at month 11 prevents choosing the model after seeing outcomes, which is valuable. But this is not out-of-sample replication. "Survives a registered test in the same offices" is accurate; "confirms" is too strong.

**The precision looks high for 14 offices.** The paper says "a larger sample of office-months", but the meetings variation is mostly between offices. Repeated months from 14 clusters add little independent information. If the 28–66% interval does not account for clustering by office, it is too narrow. The paper should state how this was handled. With so few clusters, it should use a cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference.

**Part of the mediation is built into the outcome.** The outcome counts cases closed. Meetings produce no cases but do count in the hours denominator, if the log measure includes them (see point 4). So cutting meetings raises output per hour almost by definition. That is still a real and useful finding: the time was low-value as far as the measured output is concerned. But it is accounting, not evidence of a behavioural mechanism. The paper should say so, and should also ask whether the meetings had value that cases closed doesn't capture. The appeal overturn rate (3.2% v 3.0%) is reassuring on quality but has no confidence interval.

**The assumptions of the mediation model are strong.** Meeting cuts were not randomised. Offices with more effective managers may both have cut more meetings and improved output for other reasons. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary does not.

**Where did the baseline meeting data come from?** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six, with no baseline. This paper reports a baseline of 7.4 hours in treated offices and 7.2 in control. If calendar history was recovered retrospectively, the paper should say how, and whether it was complete.

## 4. What do the system logs measure?

"Active log-in time on the case-management system" could mean either of two things:

- **All working time while logged in, including meetings.** The 11% fall on logs, close to the 12% on timesheets, suggests this reading.
- **Time spent on cases only.** If so, treated offices' measured hours should have fallen much less, because about 3.3 fewer hours per week went to meetings.

The definition affects both the 8.5% estimate and the mediation model, because the meetings pathway works through the hours denominator. One sentence would settle it. The paper should also say when the log measure was added, and whether that was before or after the month-11 registration.

## 5. The Halden follow-up

**Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations contacted did not take part. Organisations that reverted or struggled are plausibly less likely to respond. That makes the reversion rate of 3 in 14 a probable underestimate and the 11.8% gain a probable overestimate.

**The reversions are not all coverage-related.** The Summary says all three were "client-facing or coverage". But the marketing agency cited client deadlines, and the meta-analysis would code marketing as discretionary work. The body describes this accurately; the Summary should too.

**No within-organisation trajectory.** The 96.8 figure at 24 months comes from a different subset than the 95.4 at month six (17 organisations). Report the same organisations at 6 and 24 months; that is the decay test these data can actually support.

**Calling 11.8% an "upper bound" is loose.** The bias from self-selection and survivorship runs upward. But a two-year before–after comparison with no control group also picks up general productivity growth and new tools. That is another upward bias, which the paper does not mention, and there could be downward biases it hasn't considered. "Likely an overestimate" is safer than "upper bound".

## 6. Still missing

- **Backlog measures for case-processing.** The nine-month report flagged backlogs exceeding statutory deadlines as a risk, and the 24-month report still gives no queue sizes or deadline-compliance figures.
- **Confidence intervals for secondary outcomes.** Sick days, resignations and appeal overturn rates are still raw comparisons.
- **The counter-arm cost estimate.** It rests on an assumption the paper doesn't state. 12% more staff producing a 9% rise in cost per contact implies labour is about 75% of the cost of each contact. The paper should state that.

## 7. Section 5 is fair

- **On the re-analysis.** The response to Varga and Holm is proportionate. It credits their critique of the measurement problems and rejects only "entirely an artifact". Varden at 24 months does meet most of their recommended standards. One small correction: they extrapolated *energy* returning to baseline "around month ten" (my calculation gave about 8.7). They did not claim the per-hour gain itself would reach zero. The paper's paraphrase blurs that distinction.
- **On the meta-analysis.** The response is correct and important. The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, so the "no sign of decay" claim rested on exactly the designs the meta-analysis found to inflate effects.

## Where the five documents now leave things

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, well-measured | About 8–10%; at Varden, 8.5% at 24 months on logs |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | About −2% to −3%; output roughly holds |
| Per-worker output, coverage-bound work | About −9% to −11%; service worsens, and Varden ended its counter arm |
| Durability | The gain probably persists to two years and may have declined; the decline is not yet distinguishable from control-group contamination or chance |
| Mechanism | Removing low-value meeting time plausibly explains a large share; fatigue a smaller one. The meetings estimate comes from the same offices that generated the hypothesis |
| Can reorganisation without reducing hours capture the gain? | Untested; the two-office meeting audit hints that part of it can |

The most valuable next study would be a three-arm trial: reduced hours, reorganisation of meetings without reducing hours, and control. That would settle the last row, which matters most for employers.
